title: Accounting Practices and Financial Performance of Quoted Manufacturing Firms in Nigeria: Evidence from Revenue Recognition, Inventory Valuation and Depreciation Practices
summary: This study examines the relationship between selected accounting practices and the financial performance of quoted manufacturing firms in Nigeria. The study focuses on revenue recognition practices, inventory valuation methods and depreciation practices, with return on assets (ROA), operating profit margin (OPM) and return on equity (ROE) serving as the respective performance indicators. An ex-post facto design was adopted, using secondary information derived from the published financial reports of selected quoted manufacturing firms. The reported sample comprises Lafarge Africa Plc, BUA Group and Dangote Group. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis and simple regression models were employed. The reported results indicate positive and statistically significant relationships between revenue recognition practices and ROA (R = 0.748; R² = 0.559; β = 0.580; t = 5.999; p < 0.001), inventory valuation methods and OPM (R = 0.786; R² = 0.618; β = 0.691; t = 6.118; p & lt; 0.001), and depreciation practices and ROE (R = 0.804; R² = 0.646; β = 0.742; t = 6.761; p & lt; 0.001). The findings suggest that accounting policy choices and their implementation are associated with reported financial performance in the firms covered by the study. The study recommends stronger compliance with applicable financial reporting requirements, robust internal controls over revenue recognition, effective inventory systems, and periodic review of depreciation policies. title: Factors affecting audit quality in government internal audit institutions: The roles of independence, workload, and auditor specialization
summary: Audit quality plays a critical role in strengthening government internal oversight and enhancing accountability in the management of public resources. Nevertheless, recurring audit findings indicate that maintaining high-quality audits remains a challenge within APIP institutions. This study examines the effects of auditor independence, workload, and auditor specialization on audit quality among auditors of the Inspectorate General of the Ministry of Public Works. A quantitative approach was employed using primary data collected through a survey of 109 auditors. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results reveal that auditor independence and auditor specialization positively and significantly influence audit quality, whereas workload has a significant negative effect. Among the examined factors, auditor independence emerged as the strongest determinant of audit quality. These findings suggest that improving audit quality requires not only the enhancement of technical competencies but also the preservation of professional objectivity and effective workload management. This study contributes to the public sector auditing literature by providing empirical evidence on the determinants of audit quality within government internal audit institutions, particularly in the infrastructure sector, which remains underexplored in previous studies.

title: Negative press coverage, litigation risk, and audit opinions in China
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether and why auditors are more likely to issue modified audit opinions (MAOs) to clients receiving negative news reports. Design/methodology/approach Exploiting a legal regime change in China in 2005 that significantly increased auditor litigation risk, the authors divide the sample period into two subperiods: the low litigation risk period (2001–2004) and the high litigation risk period (2006–2009). The authors manually read and code all newspapers to identify firm-years in which clients received negative press coverage. To address endogeneity and self-selection concerns, the authors use propensity score matching, instrumental variable estimation and Heckman’s two-stage model. Findings This study finds that auditors are more likely to issue MAOs to clients receiving negative news reports in the high litigation risk period. In particular, auditors’ MAOs are positively related to the first negative news reports, accounting-related negative press coverage and negative news reports from state-owned media in the high litigation risk period. Further analysis shows that negative news reports increase the probability of covered firms receiving regulatory sanctions or getting sued. As a strategic defense, auditors can reduce the probability of being sued and making litigation payments by issuing MAOs in the high litigation risk period. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first to provide comprehensive evidence in support of the strategic view and its implications (negative news reports increase the probability of covered firms getting sued and auditors can mitigate litigation risk by issuing MAOs).

title: Perceived Effectiveness of Finance and Accounts Practices in a Precision Automotive Components Manufacturer: A Questionnaire-Based Study with a Proposed Finance–Operations MIS Dashboard
summary: Manufacturing finance functions are expected to do more than record transactions; they must supply timely, accurate and decision-relevant information to production, procurement and senior management. This study examines the perceived effectiveness of finance and accounts (F&A) practices in a precision automotive components manufacturer in Jamshedpur, India, using a fifteen-item, five-point Likert questionnaire that covers seven dimensions: financial reporting and accounting controls, taxation and compliance, budgeting and variance analysis, management information system (MIS) and decision support, cost analysis, digital integration and automation, and people and coordination. The research context is built from industry data and a review of recent literature on the digitalisation of management accounting, enterprise resource planning (ERP) and business intelligence, and Industry 4.0 in automotive manufacturing. Descriptive statistics and cross-tabulation are applied to a simulated demonstration dataset of 48 respondent records. The dataset is disclosed as simulated throughout and is intended to illustrate the analytical method, not to evidence the actual performance of any organisation. In the demonstration dataset, financial reporting and accounting controls recorded the highest theme mean (4.17), followed by taxation and compliance (3.98), cost analysis (3.88), people and coordination (3.85), MIS and decision support (3.83), budgeting and variance analysis (3.66) and digital integration and automation (3.49); the overall mean was 3.85. Perceived MIS timeliness differed by role, with managers rating it higher than executives. The paper proposes a phased Finance–Operations MIS dashboard that prioritises data integration, driver-based budgeting and exception-based alerts, and it offers a replicable instrument for future studies with authenticated data. title: Digital Transformation of HR Operations in Small, Field-Force-Driven Cosmeceutical Firms: A Conceptual Framework and Research Propositions Based on Secondary Evidence
summary: Purpose: Digital human resource management (e-HRM) has been studied mostly in large and multinational organisations. This paper examines how HR digitalisation can be understood in a different setting: a small, field-force-driven firm in India's cosmeceutical and therapeutic-aesthetics segment, where a compact HR team supports employees who spend most of their time outside the office. Design/approach: The paper is conceptual. It combines published market estimates, the recent Indian regulatory changes that affect HR data and employment practice, and established technology-adoption theory (the Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations and socio-technical systems theory). The authors' internship context in an HR department of one such firm motivates the questions asked, but no primary survey or interview data are reported. Findings: Market sources agree on direction but not on size: estimates of India's HRMS and HR-technology market in 2024–25 range from about USD 0.87 billion to USD 1.2 billion, with projected growth rates from 7.56% to 17.34% a year. At the same time, the Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 are turning HR systems from an administrative convenience into compliance infrastructure. The paper develops a framework and five testable propositions on ease of use in field conditions, the sequence of HRMS coverage, onboarding and training, compliance, and data quality. Originality and limitations: The paper offers a context-specific framework for an under-studied type of organisation. Because it reports no primary data, the propositions are untested; a research design for testing them is outlined. title: Artificial intelligence adoption and ethical governance in sustainable financial decision making among listed firms in the Gulf Cooperation Council
summary: This study advances the intelligent-accounting literature by examining how AI-based tools embedded in accounting systems shape sustainable financial decision-making in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) listed firms. Using a panel of 52 listed firms across the six GCC states over 2015–2024, the study apply the two-step system generalized method of moments (system GMM) to address dynamic persistence and endogeneity. Sustainable financial decision-making (SFD-M), proxied by ESG performance, is dynamic and path dependent: the lagged dependent variable is positive and significant across specifications. AI tools adoption (AI-TA) has a positive effect on SFD-M that is marginally significant, offering suggestive rather than conclusive evidence that AI-enabled accounting systems support more sustainability-oriented decisions. The digitalization index (DI) is insignificant in baseline models, indicating that digital infrastructure alone does not improve sustainability outcomes without complementary capabilities. Mechanism tests provide only weak evidence that AI-TA and DI raise accounting intelligence (AC-INT) or data quality (DQ), proxied by earnings quality; the estimated technology–mechanism links are positive in sign for AI-TA but statistically insignificant. In the full dynamic model neither DQ nor AC-INT is a significant direct driver of SFD-M, and bootstrapped indirect effects through both mechanisms are statistically indistinguishable from zero, so the data do not support the proposed mediation. Moderation analysis shows that ethical governance (EG) significantly strengthens the sustainability payoff of accounting intelligence and data quality: the AC-INT×EG and DQ×EG interactions are positive and significant even though the corresponding main effects are not. By integrating direct, mediated, and moderated pathways within a dynamic panel, the study offers theory-based and practical guidance for AI-driven sustainable finance in emerging markets.

title: Holcim Costa Rica: investing in the circular economy
summary: Learning outcomes The case aims at achieving the following learning objectives: Case overview/synopsis At the end of 2023 Julián Montero CFO of Holcim Costa Rica had to complete the financial analysis of an investment of nearly 8.975m of Costa Rican Colones (CRC), or about US$16.5m, at the company′s site in Cartago. The investment was aimed at substituting fossil fuels (Petcoke) used in the production of cement for residential residues (Municipal Solid Waste or MSW) to be sourced from a landfill site 30 km away. If implemented, the Cartago site would become the Holcim cement plant in the region with the highest proportion of alternative fuels employed as an energy source in the production cement. The environmental and social benefits of the so-called Thermal Substitution Rate (TSR) project were quite strong. The project was also aligned with Holcim’s goal of reaching a net zero target of CO2 emissions by 2050. However, the financial desirability of the investment had not been established yet. In particular, the returns from the TSR investment depended crucially upon the humidity content of the Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) that could be achieved, as well as on the prevailing price of Petcoke in international markets, among other variables. With only a few days left to submit the 2024 CAPEX budget for approval to headquarters in Switzerland, Julián was eager to determine the expected return from the TSR investment. Complexity academic level The case can be used in corporate finance courses, courses on the analysis of investment projects, capital budgeting, as well as in sustainability and ESG-related courses. The case is suitable for both degree-granting programs (graduate or undergraduate) and executive education programs. It is best suited for an audience familiar with scenario analysis and Montecarlo simulation, as it involves applying these techniques to assess the potential returns from a CAPEX investment. title: Sustainable Marketing Practices: Balancing Profitability and Environmental Responsibility
summary: The growing need to protect the environment, legal and regulatory demands, and changing consumer views have increased the pressure on companies to make their marketing strategies more sustainable. This essay discusses the concept of sustainable marketing as an integrated approach that shows how businesses can balance making profits with caring for the environment. It includes new ideas like corporate social responsibility, how different stakeholders respond, and creating value together. The paper shows how companies can work towards achieving both a competitive advantage and environmental responsibility at the same time. Sustainable marketing is not about slowing down growth, but about using it as a smart strategy that can improve brand value, customer loyalty, and long-term efficiency. Based on a detailed review of recent studies, the paper highlights three important parts of effective sustainable marketing: clearly sharing information about environmental actions, creating innovative designs for eco-friendly products and services, and working closely with supply chains to reduce carbon footprints. The paper also talks about the challenge of balancing short-term profit goals with the costs of making sustainable changes and how green consumers can help recover those costs. Moreover, the paper shows how companies are changing the way they combine profitability with environmental responsibility because of digital platforms, data analysis, and circular economy models. The research shows that companies that have truly committed to sustainability, with programs that are measurable, honest, and adaptable, are more likely to succeed in unpredictable markets. This paper adds to the conversation about business sustainability by creating a framework that brings environmental responsibility into the marketing mix. Finally, it concludes that sustainable marketing is not just a smart business choice, but also a moral duty for success in today’s market.

title: Personnel training for the digital construction industry: economic aspects
summary: The digital transformation of the construction industry is one of the key areas for improving the efficiency of investment and construction activities. The introduction of building information modeling technologies, digital twins, artificial intelligence, automated project management systems and other digital tools requires qualified specialists who are able to work in a digital economy. At the same time, the construction sector is facing a shortage of personnel with the necessary digital competencies. The article examines the economic aspects of personnel training for the digital construction industry, analyzes the causes of personnel shortages, examines the costs of training and corporate staff development, and evaluates the effectiveness of investments in improving employee digital literacy. Special attention is paid to the issues of interaction between educational organizations and construction companies as the main mechanism for the formation of human resources in the industry. Based on the analysis, promising models of cooperation between universities and employers are proposed, ensuring an increase in the quality of specialist training and a reduction in personnel shortages.

title: ESG Performance, Disclosure and Environmental Intensity: Implications for Profitability in Emerging Market Energy Companies
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between ESG performance, environmental intensity, greenwashing, and profitability in energy companies operating in emerging markets. An unbalanced panel of 95 publicly listed companies from Asia, Europe, and Latin America over 2015–2024 is analyzed using dynamic panel‐data models. ESG performance is found to be positively associated with profitability, while environmental intensity exerts a negative effect. The positive impact of ESG performance is stronger in larger companies, suggesting that organizational scale enhances the benefits derived from sustainability initiatives. Greenwashing, measured as the gap between ESG disclosure and ESG performance, is negatively associated with profitability, indicating that sustainability claims are penalized when they are not supported by actual ESG outcomes. The results also show that the COVID‐19 pandemic and the Russia‐Ukraine conflict reduced the profitability penalty associated with greenwashing. The findings highlight the importance of disclosure credibility and ESG performance in emission‐intensive industries.

title: Standardized Isolation Precautions and Infection Control Governance for High Risk Clinical Units
summary: Abstract: This health sector policy proposal establishes a standardized operational protocol for personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance and infection control across high risk clinical environments, including cardiovascular, oncology, and intensive care units. Addressing clinical variation, supply chain inefficiencies, and Joint Commission accreditation risks, the policy outlines rigid PPE donning and doffing workflows, interunit clinical handoff communications, and mandatory escalation pathways. The accompanying financial impact analysis projects that an estimated 15% increase in PPE utilization and upfront investments in automated auditing yield substantial returns on investment by mitigating uncompensated care costs and readmission penalties associated with hospital acquired infections ($20,000–$40,000 saved per avoided infection).

title: Smart Food Systems: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Digital Technologies for Food Safety and Nutrition
summary: Food safety hazards, persistent nutritional inequalities, and increasingly complex supply chains continue to challenge global food systems. Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), and related digital technologies offer new opportunities to strengthen food monitoring, traceability, quality assurance, and nutritional management. However, applications remain fragmented, and evidence linking improved technical performance to measurable food safety and nutritional outcomes is limited. This critical narrative review examines the applications, complementary functions, and practical limitations of these technologies across modern food systems, with particular attention to predictive contamination detection, automated quality assessment, supply chain transparency, nutritional monitoring, and decision support. The review identifies recurring challenges related to data reliability, limited external validation, interoperability, implementation costs, cybersecurity, and unequal access to digital infrastructure. It further distinguishes technological capabilities demonstrated under controlled conditions from sustained improvements in food safety, dietary quality, and public health in operational settings. To address these challenges, the review proposes an Integrated Digital Intelligence Framework organized around six interconnected functions (sense, integrate, analyse, verify, act, and evaluate) that links digital information and predictive intelligence with coordinated interventions, institutional accountability, and outcome evaluation. Priorities for future research include prospective multisite validation, comparative effectiveness studies against conventional systems, standardised reporting, cost-effectiveness analysis, and equity-focused implementation. Meaningful digital transformation of food systems requires moving beyond technological adoption toward integrated, evidence-based approaches that demonstrably improve food safety, nutrition, accessibility, and accountability.

title: How to overcome the productivity pains of digital transformation? The U‑shaped TFP trajectory of Chinese agricultural firms, fixed‑asset constraints and subsidy threshold effects
summary: Digital transformation has profoundly reshaped agricultural production systems, yet its productivity effects remain insufficiently explored. Using panel data of Chinese listed agricultural firms from 2010 to 2022, this paper examines the effects, mechanisms, moderation, and heterogeneity of digital transformation on total factor productivity (TFP). First, digital transformation exerts a significant U-shaped nonlinear effect on TFP: the linear coefficient is −0.154 ( p < 0.01), and the squared coefficient is 0.036 ( p < 0.01), indicating that early-stage fixed asset accumulation, organizational restructuring, and system adaptation frictions drag down TFP, while after crossing the critical threshold, network synergy and factor allocation optimization drive sustained TFP growth. Second, the fixed asset-to-revenue ratio serves as a key transmission channel, forming a nonlinear mediation path of “digitalization → fixed asset-to-sales ratio → TFP.” Bootstrap tests show that the indirect effect turns from negative to positive as digitalization increases and is significant only at high levels. Third, government subsidies significantly moderate the U-shaped relationship, shifting the turning point leftward and increasing curvature, reflecting a “turning point forward shift and dividend amplification” mechanism. Fourth, the U-shaped relationship is more pronounced for non-state-owned, small-scale, and livestock enterprises. Theoretically, this paper constructs a nonlinear mediation framework of “digitalization–asset structure–TFP,” reveals the inverted U-shaped transmission of the fixed asset-to-revenue ratio, identifies the nonlinear moderating role of government subsidies, and enriches research on digital transformation and agricultural TFP. Practically, it suggests establishing a “pain period” tolerance mechanism, shifting subsidies toward soft support, and precisely supporting non-state-owned, small-scale, and livestock enterprises to release productivity dividends.

title: Explainable AI Assisted Smart Contract Auditing for Administrative Workflows
summary: Abstract Smart contracts can encode administrative approvals, payments and record transitions, yet a valid transaction may still breach an institution’s intended procedure. This exploratory paper proposes an explainable AI-assisted auditing framework that separates vulnerability detection, explanation, repair generation and independent repair verification. A focused review of primary research and official documentation informs a workflow specification, threat model and reproducible evaluation protocol. Static analysis and transaction-oriented testing supply program evidence, while AI helps relate code to approved administrative requirements. Explanations identify the affected rule, source statements, state conditions and supporting evidence. Candidate repairs are assessed against frozen specifications, protected regression tests and applicable formal properties. An illustrative payment case shows why preventing a prohibited action is insufficient when the same change blocks legitimate activity. The proposed evaluation compares conventional auditing, AI assistance, evidence-linked explanations and independent verification under matched budgets. Detection accuracy, explanation fidelity, repair acceptance, workflow preservation and cost are measured separately. The contribution is a requirements-centred design and evaluation protocol; no prototype results or institutional field observations are claimed. title: ASSESSING THE IMPACT OF BANKING FINTECH INNOVATION ON BANK SELECTION BEHAVIOUR: EVIDENCE FROM DUAL BANKING MARKETS IN INDONESIA
summary: This study examines the effects of Banking Fintech and Financial Literacy on Banking Consumer Behaviour, with Perceived Bank Risk as an intervening variable within Indonesia’s dual banking system. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted involving 500 banking customers, including conventional and Islamic bank users. Data were collected using a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The analysis included measurement model assessment, structural model evaluation, direct effects, and mediation analysis using 5,000 bootstrap samples. The results show that Banking Fintech significantly affects Perceived Bank Risk (β = 0.178; p = 0.021) and Banking Consumer Behaviour (β = 0.349; p < 0.001). Financial Literacy significantly affects Perceived Bank Risk (β = 0.302; p < 0.001) and has the strongest direct effect on Banking Consumer Behaviour (β = 0.505; p < 0.001). Perceived Bank Risk also significantly affects Banking Consumer Behaviour (β = 0.107; p < 0.001). Furthermore, Perceived Bank Risk significantly mediates the effects of Banking Fintech (β = 0.019; p = 0.048) and Financial Literacy (β = 0.032; p = 0.003) on Banking Consumer Behaviour. The findings highlight the importance of financial capability and digital banking innovation in shaping banking consumer behaviour.

title: Behavioural Biases and Retail Investor DecisionMaking: The Moderating Role of Financial Literacy in Emerging Markets — A Critical Review
summary: ABSTRACT: Retail participation in emerging capital markets has expanded alongside mobile trading, low-cost brokerage, digital financial services and easier access to market information. These changes have made individual investors more visible in capital-market activity while increasing the importance of understanding how psychological tendencies shape decisions. This review examines the ways in which overconfidence, herding, anchoring, loss aversion, the disposition effect, representativeness, availability, mental accounting, regret aversion and affect influence retail investment decisions in emerging-market settings. It integrates behavioural-finance theory with evidence on financial literacy, investor experience, social influence, market volatility, digital platforms and institutional context. The review is organised around a transparent PRISMA 2020-aligned protocol and a structured evidence-extraction framework. Because a complete, auditable export from bibliographic databases was not available during preparation of this draft, numerical screening totals, study-frequency counts and pooled effect estimates are not fabricated. Instead, the paper provides a reproducible protocol, a critical thematic synthesis, an evidence-mapping scheme and statistical procedures that can be executed after the final eligible-study set is verified. The literature suggests that biases are neither uniform nor independent: they may interact with risk perception, financial knowledge, market sentiment, social networks and trading technology. Survey-based studies frequently report associations between self-reported biases and investment choices, but cross-sectional designs, convenience samples, common-method variance and inconsistent construct measures limit causal interpretation and cross-country comparison. The paper proposes an integrated model in which individual biases affect investment decisions directly and indirectly through risk perception and sentiment, while financial literacy, experience; digital information quality and market conditions may moderate these relationships. Its contribution is a critical, context-sensitive synthesis and an analysis plan designed to support reproducible future reviews rather than an unsupported claim of statistical meta-analysis. title: Enterprise Data Governance Combining Federated Transfer Learning and Security Audit
summary: Due to the problems of dispersed business data, inconsistent regulatory interpretations and limited cross-domain modeling at the enterprise level, this paper puts forward a data governance model based on federated transfer learning and security auditing. The preprocessing stage adds salted pseudonymization, entity masking, rare-category pooling, 30-minute window aggregation, and lineage/access-log feature construction to ensure reproducibility without revealing raw records. The method builds metadata, lineage, access behavior and rule-hitting features locally in each business domain and achieves cross-domain knowledge transfer via transfer gating and alignment loss. At the same time, it records summary hashing, responsible parties, policy consistency and lineage continuity in audit quality scores, adds a risk-suppression aggregation mechanism, and synchronously links the model update process to the governance traceability process. Experiments are based on financial, procurement, logistics, sales and compliance data from a large local group from January 2024 to December 2025. According to the results above, the proposed method achieves an AUC of 0.957, a macro-F1 score of 0.912, a recall of 0.926, and an audit trace completeness of 0.987. It is 2.1 and 2.3 percentage points higher than the best-performing comparative method. Extra imbalance, threshold-sensitivity and edge deployment tests show that the transfer gate reduces negative transfer in a 1:50 class imbalance, and audit-suppressed aggregation maintains real-time latency below 160ms under the tested edge configuration. Thus, cross-domain risk identification and strategy implementation can be achieved in a closed-loop manner without aggregating raw data, and a technical path for enterprise data governance that balances accuracy, compliance, and feasibility has been provided. A separate public HDFS log benchmark supplies a limited proxy stress test; it does not validate enterprise audit completeness or reproduce an accuracy advantage over FedAvg.

title: Accounting for Competing Events in Longitudinal Studies of Geriatric Outcomes
summary: BACKGROUND: In time-to-event analyses of geriatric outcomes, competing events such as mortality are common but are often handled inappropriately, leading to biased risk estimates and potentially incorrect inferences. We present a case study illustrating the consequences of failing to account for competing events and review how such analyses are conducted in recent JAGS publications. METHODS: For the case study, we analyzed data from the Precipitating Events Project to estimate the risk and rate of two geriatric outcomes-injurious falls and restricted activity-using methods that appropriately account for competing events and, for comparison, methods that assume competing events are absent. For the literature review, we searched PubMed for eligible JAGS articles in 2024 and assessed whether and how competing events were addressed in analyses of risk and rate. RESULTS: In the case study, we demonstrate that methods that failed to account for competing events produce inflated estimates of risk and potentially misleading differences across strata of independent variables. Also, when competing events are present, the statistical significance of the association between an independent variable and outcome rate and risk, respectively, was not consistently concordant. In the literature review, only 47% of articles reported analyses of both risk and rate, and terminology used to describe risk analyses often limited interpretation. CONCLUSIONS: Failure to properly account for competing events in longitudinal studies of geriatric outcomes can result in biased risk estimates and incorrect inferences. Clearer reporting of time-to-event analyses would strengthen the rigor and interpretability of scientific reports in the geriatric literature.

title: Identity verification in virtual shareholders’ meetings: normative foundations and legal consequences
summary: Abstract The digital transformation of corporate governance has rendered virtual shareholders’ meetings a permanent feature of modern company law. While electronic participation enhances accessibility and cross-border engagement, it raises fundamental questions concerning the reliable identification of participants. This article examines identity verification in virtual shareholders’ meetings of private limited companies under Estonian law, with comparative references to German law. The analysis is based on the understanding that identity verification is not a mere technical formality but constitutes a structural precondition for the lawful formation of the company’s collective will. Although Estonian law permits electronic participation by default, it does not prescribe any specific authentication standards. The legal requirement that only shareholders or duly authorised representatives may exercise membership rights therefore remains unchanged, while the technical means used to ensure compliance vary. The article adopts a functional perspective on identity verification. It examines different forms of authentication that may be used in virtual meetings, including the Estonian state e-identity, other digital identification means (such as those recognised under the eIDAS framework), as well as situations where no formal digital identification is available. The discussion highlights how varying degrees of technical reliability may influence legal certainty and the protection of participation rights. Particular attention is given to the legal consequences of defective identification. Drawing on Estonian case law concerning digital signatures, the article analyses the presumption arising from the use of electronic identification tools, the formal requirements of representation, and the distinction between void votes and the revocation or nullity of resolutions. It argues that identity verification serves a procedural legitimising function and does not replace the substantive determination of share ownership. Virtual meetings therefore require not the creation of new legal principles but a careful functional adaptation of established company-law concepts to a technologically mediated environment.

title: Phantom Convergence: Auditing Cross-Domain Claims in an Autonomously Built Knowledge Graph
summary: Autonomous knowledge-graph builders often report that independent sources converge on the same idea. We audited one such system, ANIMUS, three times, and each audit removed the effect the previous version reported. First, 52% of its self-reported nodes were undetected duplicates (1,892 reported, 911 unique). Second, its headline convergence, failure → algorithm "confirmed by 32 sources", co-occurs in 2 of 29 books when chance alone predicts 2.6. Of 639 co-occurring tension–resolution pairs, 4 survive a chance model with false-discovery control: fixed expressions such as problem → solution. The fourth is a topical pair, poverty → education. Third, we rebuilt the system to make such errors detectable. ANIMUS v5 extracts ideas with a local LLM, keeps an idea only if the model's verbatim quote is found in the passage, and embeds ideas with a multilingual model that passes a positive control at 97% (chance: 5%). It then counts cross-book links against decoys run through the identical procedure. On 10,392 verified ideas from 29 books (52 million cross-book pairs), real ideas produce fewer links than word-shuffled decoys (18,258 vs. 20,050). The most striking surviving theme, statements about the limits of knowledge across Kuhn, Meadows, Isaiah and Gödel-themed texts, was largely a negation artifact: both-negated pairs made up 42% of the top 100 links under word-shuffled decoys and 11% under decoys that preserve sentence form. We find no evidence of cross-domain convergence in this corpus beyond vocabulary, topic and syntax. We contribute two open-source auditing tools and a reusable recipe: quote-grounded extraction, an embedding positive control, and form-preserving decoys.
